Topic: Does a democratic majority's vote to expand its own power over the economy deserve any more deference than a dictator's decree, when both equally override the rule of law that protects the individual?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
A majority is a number of heads counted; it is not a truth, and it possesses no more sanctity than the sword of a prince, for both are merely the instruments by which men who hold power take what they can hold. I have written that men judge princes by results, not by titles or procedures — and the same rule binds assemblies. A vote that strips away the settled expectations on which a merchant, a lender, a family has built its life is a conquest like any other; it merely conquers by plebiscite rather than by garrison. The rule of law is not sacred parchment — it is the accumulated *stato*, the structure of trust that lets a people prosper without daily terror, and whoever unmakes it, whether crowned or elected, commits the same offense against order. Legitimacy of origin does not launder the illegitimacy of the act.

A dictator's decree and a majority's vote are both naked force; only their disguises differ, and only their consequences — stability preserved or squandered — should decide our judgement of them.

*The ballot box breaks no law that the sword could not break just as well — ask not who struck, but what was left standing.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
A democratic majority is still a majority, and I have never worshipped numbers where numbers do wrong: government founded on usurped power owes the people nothing more than one founded on the impudence of a court. The very idea that a law should be binding upon those it has not been drawn from by right, not merely by count, is the whole of my objection to hereditary succession — and it applies with equal force to elective despotism. A vote to strip the individual of property or liberty by simple majority is a mob with paperwork; it has exchanged the sword for the ballot but kept the plunder. Rights are not proposals to be voted up or down each generation — society did not create them, and a legislature, however chosen, cannot repeal what precedes government itself. My verdict: a majority that legislates away the rights it was formed to protect is as illegitimate as any crown, and deserves precisely the same resistance.

*A government that can vote away your rights was never a government of rights at all, only a monarchy that counts heads instead of crowning one.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The multitude, once assembled to vote, is no less a Multitude than before—their number does not dissolve them into one Person with one Will, unless they have first covenanted to be bound by the major part, and even then the covenant holds only because each severally consented to it in the beginning. A democracy that "expands its power" by simple appetite, ignoring the very laws and covenants that constituted it as Sovereign, is not exercising sovereignty but dissolving it—returning its subjects toward the condition of nature where every man's right extends to everything, which is war. The dictator's decree and the majority's unlawful vote are, in this one respect, identical acts: both are the Sword striking down the compact that alone made obedience reasonable, and I have never granted that counting heads changes the nature of the wound. What restrains either is not the shape of the assembly but whether it remembers itself bound by its own foundational Laws of Nature—equity, keeping of covenants, the safety of the people as the supreme law.

**A crowd that breaks its own covenant is not the people speaking, but the people at war with themselves.**
Keynes — Judgement:
This question assumes the rule of law is a fixed boundary equidistant from every government, but law is only the servant of whatever ends a community sets for itself — and a democracy amending its own arrangements is not the same act as a tyrant seizing new ones.

I told Hayek, on reading his Road to Serfdom, that he was tilting at a logical slope while ignoring the moral substance beneath it: planning is not dangerous in itself, only in the wrong hands pursuing wrong purposes. A majority that expands its own economic power retains the discipline of consent, argument, and the ballot's power of recall — it can reverse itself next Tuesday. A dictator's decree answers to nothing but his own will, and that asymmetry is the whole difference the abstraction "override of law" flattens out.

A vote is not a decree, because a vote remains a question the community can still ask again.

*The rule of law protects us from power that need never answer for itself, not from power that must be renewed by consent each time it is exercised.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
A majority that votes itself unlimited power over property and trade is exercising the same *appetite for arbitrary dominion* I condemned in every hereditary tyrant — the numbers change, the vice does not. I have always argued that no authority is legitimate merely because it is strong or popular; reason, not consent alone, must sanction it, for a mob can be as despotic as a monarch when it forgets that rights precede its own resolutions. The individual's claim to the fruits of their own faculties is not a privilege parliaments dispense and retract at will — it is anterior to the vote, as much a birthright as the liberty of conscience I demanded be extended to women. A vote to seize what law was instituted to protect is not self-government; it is self-government's suicide, dressed in the language of democracy to disguise the same old appetite for unaccountable power.

**VERDICT:** A democratic majority that overrides the rule of law to expand its own economic power has forfeited its claim to legitimacy exactly as a dictator has, for both substitute will for reason.

*Numbers do not sanctify tyranny; they only multiply its authors.*
